findings.title: Malicious implant p.exe executing from staging directory as Domain Admin
findings.description: p.exe (PID 8260) found at c:\windows\temp\perfmon\p.exe — a non-standard staging path mimicking a legitimate Windows perfmon directory. Process is running under the spsql account which holds Domain Admin SID (S-1-5-21-3445421715-2530590580-3149308974-512). SHA256 confirmed via mcp__hash_file; zero YARA matches from operative ruleset (informative: process dump rather than raw binary).

evidence.raw_tool_output: 8260 p.exe c:\windows\temp\perfmon\p.exe | spsql S-1-5-21-...-512 Domain Admins | sha256: 6f9d6ec7...

findings.title: WMI-based remote execution: WmiPrvSE.exe spawned PowerShell
findings.description: powershell.exe (PID 8712) was spawned by WmiPrvSE.exe (PID 2876), indicating WMI-based lateral movement or remote execution. This is the initial foothold on rd01 — an attacker-controlled WMI command triggered the PowerShell execution chain that ultimately ran p.exe. WmiPrvSE spawning PowerShell is a well-known lateral movement indicator.

findings.title: PowerShell C2 shell with stealth flags: SysWOW64 -NoLogo -NoProfile -s
findings.description: powershell.exe (PID 5848) running from SysWOW64 (32-bit process on 64-bit system) with stealth flags: -Version 5.1 -s -NoLogo -NoProfile. The -s flag indicates stdin-based command input (typical of remote C2 shells). Running as spsql with Domain Admin SID. Process has been active since 2018-08-30 16:43:42 UTC — over 8 hours before the memory capture — and spawned six rundll32 instances and the p.exe delivery cmd.exe.

findings.title: Active C2 channel to 172.16.4.10:8080 — multiple connections
findings.description: netscan reveals multiple TCP connections from 172.16.6.11 to 172.16.4.10:8080, including ESTABLISHED and numerous CLOSE_WAIT/CLOSED states, indicating sustained C2 beaconing over HTTP(S) port 8080. Connections are orphaned (PID=-) in the netscan snapshot, consistent with p.exe managing connections through the network stack without a direct socket handle visible at scan time.

findings.title: spsql account with Domain Admin privileges used as attacker context
findings.description: Both p.exe (PID 8260) and the PowerShell C2 shell (PID 5848) execute under the spsql account which holds SID S-1-5-21-3445421715-2530590580-3149308974-512 (Domain Admins) and S-1-5-32-544 (Administrators). This indicates the attacker had compromised a Domain Admin service account, giving them unrestricted access across the domain.

evidence.raw_tool_output: 8260 p.exe S-1-5-21-...-512 Domain Admins | S-1-5-32-544 Administrators | High Mandatory Level

findings.title: Six rundll32.exe instances spawned by PowerShell C2 shell (PID 5848)
findings.description: Six rundll32.exe processes were spawned by powershell.exe (PID 5848) across the intrusion timeline: PIDs 6768 (2018-08-30 18:31), 5452 (21:40), 5588 (21:40), 2216 (22:31), 4108 (22:45), 8148 (2018-08-31 00:56). All exited within seconds. This pattern is consistent with in-memory shellcode staging or C2 tasking — rundll32 used as a LOLBin to execute attacker payloads without dropping new files.

findings.title: SMB lateral movement to 172.16.4.5:445 (ESTABLISHED)
findings.description: Active ESTABLISHED SMB connection from victim (172.16.6.11:49763) to 172.16.4.5:445 observed in netscan. Combined with multiple CLOSED RDP connections to the same host, this indicates the attacker moved laterally to 172.16.4.5 using both SMB file sharing and RDP sessions.

findings.title: Full attacker process chain: WmiPrvSE → PS(8712) → PS(5848) → cmd → p.exe
findings.description: Pstree reveals the complete attacker execution chain: WmiPrvSE.exe (2876) spawned powershell.exe (8712) at 16:43:36 UTC, which spawned SysWOW64 powershell.exe (5848) with stealth flags at 16:43:42 UTC, which spawned cmd.exe (5948) at 22:15:18 UTC executing p.exe. This chain documents WMI-based initial execution → C2 shell establishment → implant deployment across a 5.5-hour window on 2018-08-30.

findings.title: p.exe DLL profile: full network/crypto stack loaded; post-execution DLL loading
findings.description: windows.dlllist for p.exe (PID 8260) shows a complete network and cryptography stack: WININET.dll (HTTP/HTTPS), WS2_32.dll (Winsock), DNSAPI.dll, IPHLPAPI.DLL, SSPICLI.DLL (Kerberos/NTLM), rsaenh.dll, bcrypt.dll, CRYPTBASE.dll. Critically, mpr.dll was loaded at 2018-09-05 12:13:26 UTC — 5+ days after process start (2018-08-30 22:15:18), followed by USER32/GDI32 family at 12:14:36. Post-execution DLL loading indicates the implant remained active and received new tasking requiring additional capabilities.

evidence.dll_name: WININET.dll, WS2_32.dll, SSPICLI.DLL, rsaenh.dll, bcrypt.dll, mpr.dll
evidence.raw_tool_output: p.exe loaded: WININET(22:15:19) WS2_32(22:15:19) SSPICLI(22:15:19) bcrypt(22:15:19) | mpr.dll loaded 2018-09-05 12:13:26 UTC (5d later)

findings.title: procdump.exe staged in user's Dashlane password manager directory
findings.description: procdump.exe found at \Users\tdungan\AppData\Roaming\Dashlane\6.2.0.12026\procdump.exe — a credential dumping tool staged in an unusual location within the legitimate Dashlane password manager folder, likely to blend in with user-installed software. SHA256 confirmed via mcp__hash_file. Zero YARA matches from operative ruleset (process data dump).

findings.title: Three additional rundll32.exe instances spawned by p.exe (PID 8260)
findings.description: p.exe (PID 8260) spawned three rundll32.exe processes: PID 5768 (2018-09-05 12:01:32), PID 1424 (2018-09-06 14:58:41), PID 7552 (2018-09-06 17:26:32). All exited within seconds. These post-implant-deployment executions span over a week, confirming long-term attacker persistence and ongoing tasking through the implant.

findings.title: SMB lateral movement to 172.16.7.15:445 — second target subnet
findings.description: Active ESTABLISHED SMB connection from victim (172.16.6.11:59352) to 172.16.7.15:445 in a different subnet than 172.16.4.5, indicating the attacker used rd01 as a pivot point to reach multiple network segments.

findings.title: WinRM connection attempt to 172.16.5.21:5985
findings.description: CLOSED TCP connection from 172.16.6.11:49791 to 172.16.5.21:5985 (WinRM HTTP) in netscan, indicating the attacker attempted lateral movement via WinRM to a third target host.

findings.title: No registry-based persistence or malicious services detected
findings.description: windows.registry.printkey on Run and RunOnce keys across all loaded hives shows no attacker-installed entries. spsql ntuser.dat Run key is empty. windows.svcscan output contains no services with binaries in user-writable paths (Temp, AppData, Users). The attacker relied on an interactive session (PowerShell C2 shell) rather than installing persistent registry or service-based mechanisms.

evidence.raw_tool_output: spsql ntuser.dat Run key: no entries | RunOnce: no entries | svcscan: no services in user-writable paths

findings.title: OUTLOOK.EXE dtrR RWX region — malfind hit
findings.description: malfind flagged two RWX regions in OUTLOOK.EXE (PID 8128) containing the byte sequence 64 74 72 52 (dtrR). This is the VSTO/COM IDispatch dispatch table marker, not injected shellcode. Pattern is well-documented as a false positive in Office processes.

evidence.raw_tool_output: 8128 OUTLOOK.EXE 0x363a0000 PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE VadS | hexdump: 64 74 72 52 00 00 00 00 — dtrR pattern

findings.retraction_reason: Hexdump shows 64 74 72 52 (dtrR) — documented VSTO COM dispatch table marker present in all Office processes. Not injected code. Known false positive pattern in malfind output for Microsoft Office applications.

findings.title: UpdaterUI.exe RWX region — malfind hit
findings.description: malfind flagged a small RWX page in UpdaterUI.exe (PID 6036) containing only null bytes and low-value addresses. UpdaterUI.exe is the McAfee Agent update UI, a legitimate security product binary. The RWX page is consistent with McAfee's own memory allocation patterns.
findings.retraction_reason: UpdaterUI.exe is a McAfee Agent binary. Small RWX page contains null bytes and low addresses consistent with McAfee's memory management. No PE header, no shellcode patterns. Known false positive for endpoint security products.

findings.title: powershell.exe PID 8712 malfind hits — CLR heap false positive
findings.description: malfind flagged three RWX regions in powershell.exe (PID 8712). All three hexdumps contain the 0xEEFFEEFF marker at offset +8, which is the .NET CLR garbage collector heap sentinel value. This is a well-documented false positive for all .NET managed processes.

evidence.raw_tool_output: 8712 powershell.exe 0x1b4ce1a0000 PAGE_EXECUTE_READWRITE | hexdump: ee ff ee ff 02 00 00 00 — CLR heap marker

findings.retraction_reason: All three flagged regions contain 0xEEFFEEFF at offset +8 — the documented .NET CLR GC heap sentinel. powershell.exe is a managed .NET process; RWX CLR heap segments are expected. No injected code present. Known false positive pattern for .NET/PowerShell processes.
